transcript.text: Scarcity
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-01
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain scarcity and identify tradeoffs created by limited resources
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Scarcity means people, businesses, and governments have limited resources but unlimited wants. Because resources such as time, money, labor, and raw materials are limited, choices must be made. Every choice involves a tradeoff, and those tradeoffs force individuals and societies to decide how to use scarce resources. Scarcity is the basic problem that economics studies.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Resources are limited, but wants are greater than what can be produced.
A choice must be made between competing uses.
Getting more of one thing means giving up something else.
The question focuses on limits, tradeoffs, or unmet wants.
WATCH OUT
Scarcity does not mean there is almost none of a good. It means the good is limited relative to wants. Even time and money are scarce because they have alternative uses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING BETWEEN SCARCE USES

A student has two hours before an exam and must choose between studying economics or finishing a history paper. The student cannot fully do both. This is scarcity because time is limited, so choosing one use means giving up the other.
CHECK YOURSELF
A city has enough money to build either a new park or repair several roads, but not both this year. Why is this an example of scarcity?

transcript.text: Incentives
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-02
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Predict behavioral responses and unintended consequences created by incentives.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Incentives change the expected benefits or costs of a choice, so they can alter behavior at the margin. A congestion fee raises the cost of the next downtown trip. Incentives can be monetary or nonmonetary, and different people may respond differently. A reward can also improve a measured result while harming the underlying goal.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A speed bonus makes workers finish faster, but quality falls.
A new toll reduces traffic on a busy road.
A toll is added to a crowded bridge, and some drivers switch routes.
A school rewards high test pass rates.
An incentive changes the payoff to a choice; it need not be monetary or guarantee a result.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to define incentives as cash payments or guaranteed behavior. An incentive changes the expected payoff to a choice; it may be monetary or nonmonetary, and people can respond differently.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RESPONDING TO INCENTIVES

A city adds a $4 congestion fee for a rush-hour trip. Assume other trip costs are already deducted from each driver's benefit. A driver with a remaining benefit of $3 avoids the trip because the fee exceeds that benefit. A commuter with a remaining benefit of $10 still travels. The fee changes choices at the margin without making every driver respond alike.
CHECK YOURSELF
A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?

Return to the game and master this concept.
Opportunity Cost
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-03
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify and calculate the value of the next-best alternative.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made. Scarcity makes opportunity cost unavoidable because using time, money, or resources for one purpose prevents their use elsewhere. The cost is the single best forgone option, valued from the decision maker's perspective, and it can be monetary or nonmonetary.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a choice between two or more alternatives under a time, money, or resource constraint.
Identify the next-best alternative that the decision maker gives up.
Value the forgone alternative from the decision maker's perspective.
Do not add every rejected option; opportunity cost is the single best alternative forgone.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to add the value of every forgone option. Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative, not the sum of all alternatives.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING THE NEXT-BEST OPTION

A student can spend Saturday working for $80, studying for an exam worth an estimated $60 benefit, or attending a concert valued at $40. If the student studies, the best forgone alternative is the $80 work shift. The opportunity cost of studying is therefore $80, not $120 and not the concert's $40 value.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can spending an hour in a free park have an opportunity cost?

transcript.text: Marginal Analysis
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-04
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use marginal benefits and costs while avoiding sunk-cost reasoning.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit of the next unit or small change with its additional cost. A decision should expand while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost and stop before the next unit costs more than it adds. Sunk costs do not affect this forward-looking comparison, while costs or benefits imposed on others matter in social marginal analysis.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a decision about one more unit, one more hour, or a small change in an activity.
Compare the additional benefit of that change with its additional cost.
Continue while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost; stop before the next unit costs more than it adds.
Ignore totals or averages when the question asks whether the next unit is worthwhile.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to decide from total benefit or total cost. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and additional cost of the next unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPARING MARGINAL BENEFIT AND COST

A warehouse earns $15 from handling one additional box, and the marginal cost of that box is $13. Marginal net benefit is $15 - $13 = $2, so handling the box increases profit. If the next box cost $17 instead, its marginal net benefit would be -$2 and the warehouse should stop before that box.
CHECK YOURSELF
Total cost is $100 for 10 units, and producing an eleventh unit adds $15. Which number is average cost, and which is marginal cost?

transcript.text: Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-05
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish microeconomic and macroeconomic questions.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, workers, and individual markets. Macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation, and unemployment. One event can require both kinds of analysis. The distinction is the unit of analysis, not the size of an organization or dataset.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A report tracks national inflation, unemployment, and total output.
A firm decides how much labor to hire at one restaurant.
Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.
A bakery studies how customers respond to a muffin price increase.
Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, and specific markets.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to label any large organization as macroeconomic. The classification depends on the unit of analysis: one decision-maker is micro; economy-wide aggregates are macro.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MICRO OR MACRO?

A restaurant deciding whether to hire one more server is a microeconomic question because it concerns one firm's choice. The national unemployment rate is a macroeconomic outcome because it aggregates labor-market conditions across the economy. The subject's size is not decisive; the unit of analysis is.
CHECK YOURSELF
A national retailer studies how its own customers respond to a price increase. Is that question microeconomic or macroeconomic, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Positive vs. Normative Analysis
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-06
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Positive analysis makes claims that evidence can test, while normative analysis applies value judgments about what should be done. Identify what observation could support or contradict a testable claim. A positive claim can be false. A normative claim ranks goals or outcomes using values; evidence can inform that judgment but cannot settle the values alone.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership.
Ridership data can test the prediction even if it turns out to be wrong.
A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair.
A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer.
WATCH OUT
Do not treat positive as good, true, or politically neutral. A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.
WORKED EXAMPLE: POSITIVE OR NORMATIVE?

The statement 'A lower bus fare will increase ridership' is positive because ridership data can support or contradict it. The statement 'The city should lower bus fares because access is fair' is normative because it applies a value judgment. Evidence can inform both statements, but only the first is directly testable as written.
CHECK YOURSELF
Is every policy statement normative?

transcript.text: Models and Assumptions
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-07
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate the purpose, assumptions, simplifications, and limits of economic models.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Economic models simplify reality to isolate the relationships that matter for a particular question. The two-good abstraction exposes scarcity and opportunity cost without describing every output. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context. Extra complexity is useful only when its benefits exceed lost clarity or robustness. Apply a model where its important assumptions remain reasonable.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Adding dozens of variables improves historical fit but makes the mechanism impossible to interpret.
A central bank changes its policy rule, and a forecasting relationship estimated under the old rule breaks down.
A local haircut model omits exchange rates and global shipping.
An economist builds a simple two-market circular-flow model and leaves out banks, government, and foreign trade.
An economist studies how price affects purchases while holding income constant.
WATCH OUT
Do not use the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING A MODEL

A PPF model includes only two goods, even though real economies produce thousands. That simplification isolates scarcity and opportunity cost: moving toward more of one good requires less of the other. The model is useful for that purpose, but it would be inadequate for predicting the output of a specific industry without additional detail.
CHECK YOURSELF
What role does an assumption play in a model?

transcript.text: Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret PPF points, slopes, shifts, efficiency, growth, and opportunity cost.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A production possibilities frontier shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology. A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost: specialized resources become less well suited as production shifts toward the other good. Points inside indicate unused capacity; points outside are currently infeasible.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology.
A new technology improves only medical production.
An economy first removes unemployment, then gains new machinery.
Using idle resources changes the production point; resources or technology shift the frontier.
WATCH OUT

Do not confuse a PPF with a market curve. A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology. Using idle resources changes the production point; resources or technology shift the frontier.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING A PPF

The horizontal axis is Good X and the vertical axis is Good Y. A bowed-out frontier passes through A at (0, 50), B at (8, 45), C at (15, 35), D at (21, 20), and E at (25, 0). F is inside the frontier near (8, 20), and G is outside it near (21, 48).

On the PPF, moving from point C (15 units of X and 35 of Y) to point D (21 of X and 20 of Y) gains 6 units of X but gives up 15 units of Y. The total opportunity cost is 15 units of Y, or 15/6 = 2.5 units of Y per additional unit of X.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-09
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost, even when another producer has an absolute advantage in both goods. Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost. Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain. Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange. Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.
Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
One lamp costs Ari 2 rugs and costs Bea 6 rugs.
One producer is more productive in both goods.
Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to choose the producer with the greatest absolute output. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, and a mutually beneficial terms-of-trade ratio lies between the two opportunity costs.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE

Ari gives up 24/12 = 2 rugs per lamp; Bea gives up 60/10 = 6 rugs per lamp. Ari has comparative advantage in lamps. For rugs, Bea gives up 1/6 lamp, below Ari's 1/2 lamp. A trade of one lamp for four rugs lies between the two lamp costs, so both can gain from specializing and exchanging.
CHECK YOURSELF
If 1 X costs 2 Y, what is the cost of 1 Y?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Economists and Policy
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-10
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Analyze the economist's role in policy advice.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Economists use evidence and models to estimate policy effects, identify tradeoffs, and explain uncertainty. Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences. Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal. Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments. Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption.
Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.
A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period.
Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to give economists authority to choose society's values. Economists can estimate consequences and tradeoffs; the policy choice also requires normative judgments.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING POLICY ADVICE

An economist estimates that a proposed transit subsidy will increase ridership by 8%, but the estimate comes from a city with denser development. Professional advice reports the predicted benefit, explains the uncertain transfer to the local setting, and identifies fiscal costs. Whether those consequences justify the policy also depends on public values and priorities.
CHECK YOURSELF
An estimate from a dense city predicts an 8% ridership gain in a rural area. Which assumption about travel alternatives should the economist examine before applying that estimate?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Competitive Markets
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-11
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Identify the conditions that create price-taking behavior and limited market power
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A competitive market contains many independent buyers and sellers, usually trading products that buyers view as close substitutes. No single participant controls enough of the market to set the market price. A small firm is therefore a price taker: it chooses how much to sell at the price created by market supply and demand. Competition becomes stronger when firms can enter or exit, buyers can compare offers, and switching among sellers is easy.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Many independent firms sell the same product or close substitutes.
One seller supplies only a small share of total market output.
A firm accepts a price determined by overall market supply and demand.
Buyers can compare prices and switch sellers without much difficulty.
Entry by new firms or exit by existing firms changes competitive pressure.
WATCH OUT

A market is not strictly competitive just because it has several sellers. Product differentiation, search costs, network effects, or barriers to entry can still give firms pricing power. The key question is whether one seller can raise its price persistently without losing many customers to available alternatives.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING A PRICE TAKER

A wheat farmer is one of thousands selling a standardized crop. The posted market price is $6 per bushel. If this farmer asks $7 while other farmers still charge $6, buyers can purchase identical wheat elsewhere. The farmer is too small to move the market price, so raising the price would sharply reduce sales. The evidence - many sellers, a standardized product, and easy switching - identifies price-taking behavior.
CHECK YOURSELF
An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare, but a merger leaves one company controlling most available inventory. Which fact strengthens competition, which fact weakens it, and why?

transcript.text: Demand & the Law of Demand
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-12
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain demand, quantity demanded, and movements along a demand curve.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Demand describes the quantities buyers are willing and able to purchase at different prices, holding other demand conditions constant. Quantity demanded is the amount buyers choose at one particular price. The law of demand states that a lower own price increases quantity demanded and a higher own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same demand curve; it does not shift the curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The good's own price changes while income, tastes, expectations, related-good prices, and the number of buyers remain constant.
The question asks for quantity demanded at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same downward-sloping demand curve.
A lower price is paired with a larger quantity demanded.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to call every change in quantity a shift in demand. If the good's own price changes and buyers move from one point to another on the same demand curve, quantity demanded changes. Demand itself shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MOVEMENT ALONG DEMAND

Horizontal axis: quantity of gourmet donuts in thousands. Vertical axis: price of gourmet donuts in dollars. A downward-sloping demand curve for gourmet donuts. Point A is at price $10 and quantity 100 thousand; point B is at price $5 and quantity 225 thousand.

On the gourmet-donut graph, point A shows a price of $10 and quantity demanded of 100 thousand. Point B shows a lower price of $5 and quantity demanded of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same demand curve and only the good's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity demanded of 125 thousand, not an increase in demand.
CHECK YOURSELF
The price of a concert ticket falls and buyers move to another point on the same demand curve. What changes: demand or quantity demanded?
READY?

transcript.text: Determinants of Demand
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift demand left or right.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Demand shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Demand increases and shifts right when buyers want more at every price; demand decreases and shifts left when they want less at every price. Important determinants include income, tastes and preferences, expectations, the number of buyers, and the prices of substitutes and complements. The direction of an income effect depends on whether the good is normal or inferior, and the effect of a related-good price depends on whether the goods are substitutes or complements.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Consumer income, preferences, expectations, or the number of buyers changes.
The price of a substitute or complement changes.
Quantity demanded changes at the same price.
The entire demand curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a demand shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A nonprice determinant changes how much buyers want at every price and shifts the entire curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DEMAND SHIFT

Horizontal axis: quantity of coffee in thousands. Vertical axis: price of coffee in dollars. Two parallel coffee demand curves. D1 lies to the right of D0; at price $10, quantity demanded rises from 50 thousand on D0 to 125 thousand on D1.

At a coffee price of $10, the original curve D0 shows quantity demanded of 50 thousand, while D1 shows 125 thousand. The price of coffee is held constant, so the 75-thousand increase cannot be a movement along D0. It is a rightward shift from D0 to D1, meaning a nonprice determinant has increased demand.
CHECK YOURSELF
Income rises for buyers of a normal good. Which direction does its demand curve shift, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Supply & the Law of Supply
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain supply, quantity supplied, and movements along a supply curve.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Supply describes the quantities sellers are willing and able to offer at different prices, holding other supply conditions constant. Quantity supplied is the amount sellers offer at one particular price. The law of supply states that a higher own price generally increases quantity supplied and a lower own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same supply curve; it does not shift the curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The good's own price changes while production conditions remain constant.
The question asks for quantity supplied at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same upward-sloping supply curve.
A higher price is paired with a larger quantity supplied.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to call every change in quantity a shift in supply. If the good's own price changes and sellers move from one point to another on the same supply curve, quantity supplied changes. Supply itself shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MOVEMENT ALONG SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: quantity of coffee in thousands. Vertical axis: price of coffee in dollars. An upward-sloping coffee supply curve. Point A is at price $6 and quantity 100 thousand; point B is at price $11 and quantity 225 thousand.

On the coffee supply graph, point A shows a price of $6 and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Point B shows a higher price of $11 and quantity supplied of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same supply curve and only coffee's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity supplied of 125 thousand, not an increase in supply.
CHECK YOURSELF
The market price of handmade tables rises and sellers move to another point on the same supply curve. What changes?

transcript.text: Determinants of Supply
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-15
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift supply left or right.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Supply shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Supply increases and shifts right when sellers can provide more at every price; supply decreases and shifts left when they provide less at every price. Important determinants include input and resource costs, technology and productivity, taxes and subsidies, expectations, the number of sellers, and natural or regulatory production conditions. A change that lowers marginal production cost generally increases supply, while a change that raises marginal cost generally decreases it.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Input prices, technology, productivity, taxes, or subsidies change.
Producers' expectations or the number of sellers changes.
Quantity supplied changes at the same price.
The entire supply curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a supply shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A change in production cost, technology, expectations, or the number of sellers changes how much firms offer at every price and shifts the curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SUPPLY SHIFT

Horizontal axis: quantity of hamburgers in thousands. Vertical axis: price of hamburgers in dollars. Two parallel hamburger supply curves. S1 lies to the left of S0; at price $9, quantity supplied falls from 200 thousand on S0 to 100 thousand on S1.

At a hamburger price of $9, the original curve S0 shows quantity supplied of 200 thousand, while S1 shows 100 thousand. The product's price is unchanged, so the 100-thousand decrease is not a movement along S0. It is a leftward shift from S0 to S1, consistent with a determinant such as higher input costs reducing supply.
CHECK YOURSELF
A new technology lowers the cost of producing solar panels. Which direction does supply shift, and why?

Market Equilibrium
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price, buyers can purchase the amount they want and sellers can sell the amount they offer, so there is no pressure for price to change. A demand or supply shift creates a new intersection and can change both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
On a graph, use the intersection of the demand and supply curves.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage; a price above equilibrium creates a surplus.
Report both the equilibrium price and the corresponding equilibrium quantity.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to call any intersection or stated price an equilibrium. Equilibrium occurs only where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MARKET EQUILIBRIUM

Price in dollars is vertical; quantity in thousands is horizontal. Downward demand and upward supply intersect at E, quantity 150 and price 5. No curve shifts are shown. Above 5 supply exceeds demand; below 5 demand exceeds supply.

Demand and supply intersect at a price of $5 and quantity of 150 thousand. Buyers want exactly the amount sellers offer at that point. A price above $5 creates a surplus; a price below $5 creates a shortage. This example finds equilibrium without shifting either curve.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a price below $5 on this graph, which quantity is larger, and what pressure does that create on price?
READY?

Shortages and Surpluses
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-17
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price. Buyers competing for limited supply put upward pressure on price. A surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded; sellers then face pressure to lower price. Adjustment tends toward the price where the two quantities are equal.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
At the current price, buyers want 180 units and sellers offer 120 units.
A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to reverse shortage and price pressure. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING A SHORTAGE

The horizontal axis is quantity of gas in thousands of gallons and the vertical axis is price of gas per gallon. D0 slopes downward from price $6 at quantity 0 to quantity 300 thousand at price $0. S0 slopes upward from the origin to price $6 at quantity 300 thousand. The curves intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand. At price $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand and quantity supplied is 100 thousand. At price $4, quantity demanded is 100 thousand and quantity supplied is 200 thousand.

At a price of $2 per gallon, the graph shows quantity demanded of 200 thousand gallons and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Because buyers want 100 thousand more gallons than sellers offer, the market has a shortage of 200 - 100 = 100 thousand gallons. Upward pressure on price follows.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a price of $4, buyers want 100 thousand gallons and sellers offer 200 thousand. Calculate the imbalance and predict the pressure on price.

transcript.text: Simultaneous Shifts
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-18
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

When demand and supply shift at the same time, each shift contributes separately to the new equilibrium. Analyze how each change affects price and quantity, then combine the directional effects. If both shifts push one variable in the same direction, that result is determinate; if they push in opposite directions, the result depends on the relative size of the shifts.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Both a demand determinant and a supply determinant change.
A bicycle endorsement raises demand while higher input costs reduce supply.
Analyze each shift separately before combining its price and quantity effects.
Opposing effects on one variable leave its direction ambiguous unless relative shift sizes are known.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts. A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMBINING DEMAND AND SUPPLY SHIFTS

The horizontal axis is quantity of gas in thousands and the vertical axis is price of gas. Original demand D0 and original supply S0 intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand. Demand shifts right to D1 while supply shifts left to S1. D1 and S1 intersect at price $5 and quantity 150 thousand. Holding S0 fixed, D1 intersects S0 at price $4 and quantity 200 thousand. Holding D0 fixed, S1 intersects D0 at price $4 and quantity 100 thousand.

The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 and quantity of 150 thousand. After demand shifts right to D1 and supply shifts left to S1, the new intersection is $5 and the same quantity of 150 thousand. Both shifts raise price; their opposing quantity effects happen to offset in this graph, though quantity would otherwise be ambiguous.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which pair of market changes is shown when the graph moves from D0/S0 to D1/S1?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Price Ceilings
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-19
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding ceilings and analyze shortages and rationing.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A price ceiling sets a legal maximum price and is binding only when it lies below the market equilibrium price. A binding ceiling keeps price from rising to equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage develops. A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT

transcript.text: GDP Measurement
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-01
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply GDP inclusion rules and explain why measured expenditure equals measured income
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Gross domestic product is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific period. Current production matters: used goods, stocks, bonds, and transfer payments do not represent newly produced output. Final goods are counted instead of adding intermediate goods separately, because the intermediate value is already included in the final product. The location of production, not the owner's nationality, determines whether output is domestic. Measured expenditure equals measured income because a buyer's spending becomes income to the sellers and workers who produced the output.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The good or service was produced during the period being measured.
Production occurred inside the country's borders, regardless of ownership.
A final product is distinguished from an input used to make another product.
A resale, financial trade, or transfer changes ownership but adds no current output.
One transaction is viewed as both buyer expenditure and seller income.
WATCH OUT

Spending money does not automatically create GDP. A used-car sale, stock purchase, or cash transfer may be a transaction without current production. Also, adding the value of an intermediate input and the final good double counts the input. Imports are excluded because they were produced abroad, even when domestic residents buy them.

A mill sells flour to a bakery for $50, and the bakery sells the finished bread to households for $120. Final-goods accounting counts $120, not $170, because the flour's value is already embodied in the bread. The households' $120 of expenditure becomes revenue and income for the producers involved. Counting the same production from the expenditure side or the income side therefore gives the same GDP amount.

transcript.text: GDP Components

MACRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The expenditure approach divides GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports. Consumption covers household purchases of final goods and services; investment includes business capital, residential construction, and inventory changes; government purchases pay for current goods and services. Net exports add exports and subtract imports so GDP counts only domestic production, while transfer payments themselves are excluded. A recipient's later purchase is counted separately if it pays for current domestic output.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Classify final spending as consumption, investment, government purchases, or net exports.
Count newly produced capital goods and inventory changes as investment.
Exclude transfer payments because they are not payments for current production.
Subtract imports within net exports so foreign production is not counted in domestic GDP.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to count transfer payments as government purchases. Transfers redistribute income and are never themselves part of GDP. A later purchase is classified by what is bought; imports are subtracted in NX.

A business buys a newly produced domestic machine for $2 million; this is investment. Government pays contractors $80 million to repair roads; this is government purchases. An $80 million benefit payment is a transfer and is not counted when sent, though any later household purchase of final goods enters consumption. The expenditure identity classifies the counted spending as C + I + G + NX. These purchases contribute $2 million to I and $80 million to G, or $82 million directly to GDP; the transfer is not an additional government purchase.

Nominal GDP values current production at current prices, while real GDP values it at base-year prices. Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods. GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare. Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Nominal GDP uses current-year prices and current-year quantities.
Real GDP uses base-year prices with current-year quantities.
A change in nominal GDP can reflect prices, quantities, or both; a change in real GDP reflects quantities.
Use the GDP deflator to compare nominal GDP with real GDP for the same year.

Unpaid elder care becomes an otherwise similar paid service.
A country has higher GDP, but also more pollution and longer work hours.

Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain how prices coordinate buyers, sellers, and resource allocation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Prices coordinate decentralized decisions by communicating scarcity and changing the incentives facing buyers and sellers. Information about waiting costs can redirect users much like a price signal. A higher price raises the cost of consuming the good and encourages substitution or conservation. A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses. A supply improvement can lower price by reducing the good’s relative scarcity.

A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses.
The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads.
A congested road has no toll.
A price rises while quantity sold also rises.
A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising.

A common mistake is to assume that a higher price always tells buyers and sellers to do the same thing. It discourages quantity demanded while encouraging quantity supplied, coordinating opposite responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: USING A PRICE SIGNAL

A shortage develops at the current market price. Buyers compete for the limited units, putting upward pressure on price. As price rises, quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises, reducing the shortage. The price signal helps coordinate buyers and sellers without a central allocation decision.

The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.

Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.

Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.
Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.
A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude.
Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.
A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output.

Two price-quantity points are provided for a midpoint calculation.
The problem asks whether the quantity response is elastic, unit elastic, or inelastic.
Substitutes, time to adjust, budget share, or market scope are changing.
A linear demand curve has constant slope but different elasticity along the line.
A horizontal or vertical demand curve represents a limiting elasticity case.

A steeper-looking curve is not automatically less elastic. Slope uses the original price and quantity units, while elasticity compares percentage changes and depends on the price-quantity location. WATCH OUT
Do not confuse supply elasticity with demand shifters. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN VERSUS LONG-RUN SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Upward-sloping SR supply is steeper than upward-sloping LR supply. Both pass through quantity 60 and price 4. At price 8, point A on SR supply is at quantity 70 and point B on LR supply is at quantity 100. Dashed guides connect those values to the axes.

The price rises from $4 to $8. On the short-run curve, quantity rises from 60 to 70, so the midpoint quantity change is 10/65 = 15.4%; the midpoint price change is 4/6 = 66.7%. Short-run supply elasticity is 15.4%/66.7% = 0.23, which is inelastic. The flatter long-run curve shows a larger quantity response.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using the midpoint method, the price of artisan bread loaves changes from $4 to $5 and quantity supplied changes from 900 to 1080. What is price elasticity of supply?

transcript.text: Income Elasticity of Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-06
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Income Elasticity of Demand.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Income elasticity of demand measures how demand changes when consumer income changes. Income elasticity helps firms anticipate demand shifts as consumer income changes. Different income responses shift the composition of demand as purchasing power changes. Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income. A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises.
A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls.
A retailer estimates income elasticity for its store brand at -0.6.
Demand for a normal good rises as income rises.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to misread the sign of income elasticity. A positive coefficient identifies a normal good; a negative coefficient identifies an inferior good.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING INCOME ELASTICITY

Household income rises by 10%, and demand for restaurant meals rises by 15%. Income elasticity is 15% / 10% = 1.5. The positive sign identifies restaurant meals as a normal good, and the coefficient above 1 indicates that demand responds more than proportionally to income in this example.
CHECK YOURSELF
Income changes by 5 percent and demand for premium gym memberships changes by 8 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-07
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a price change in another good. A large positive cross-price coefficient signals a strong substitution relationship. Complementary goods connect through opposite movements between one price and the other good's demand. Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity. Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises.
Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7.
A negative cross-price coefficient means demand moves opposite the other good’s price.
The price of Product Y falls 8 percent.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse cross price with income or own price. A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING COMPLEMENTS

The price of printers rises by 10%, and demand for ink cartridges falls by 7%. Cross-price elasticity is -7% / 10% = -0.7. The negative sign indicates that printers and ink cartridges are complements because a higher price for printers reduces demand for ink.
CHECK YOURSELF
Cross-price elasticity of ink demand with respect to printer price is -0.7. If printer price falls 5%, calculate the predicted percentage change in ink demand and state its direction.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Elasticity and Total Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.
If price and total revenue move in the same direction, demand is inelastic over that range.
At unit elasticity, a small price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to compute elasticity without checking the associated total-revenue change. With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ELASTICITY AND REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. A straight downward-sloping Demand line runs from price 16 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 120. Its marked points are C at quantity 30, price 12; B at quantity 60, price 8; and A at quantity 90, price 4. Dashed guides show each point on both axes.

At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.
CHECK YOURSELF

Cruise-cabin price falls from $3,200 to $2,880 while quantity rises from 1,500 to 1,900. Calculate midpoint elasticity and both revenue totals. Is demand elastic over this range, and does revenue rise or fall?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Applications of Elasticity
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-09
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Apply Applications of Elasticity.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Elasticity helps predict tax incidence, deadweight loss, pricing responses, and other outcomes that depend on how strongly quantity responds. Market power is stronger when buyers have fewer substitutes. Labor demand is a derived factor demand. The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden. With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.
With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.
A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.1.
Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.
WATCH OUT

Distinguish who sends the tax payment from who bears its economic burden. The less responsive side has fewer ways to avoid the tax, so compare demand and supply elasticities before assigning the burden.
WORKED EXAMPLE: PREDICTING TAX INCIDENCE

Two sides of a market face a $6 tax. Buyers have few substitutes and reduce purchases only slightly, while sellers can redirect output to other markets. Demand is less elastic than supply, so buyers bear more of the tax through a larger increase in the price they pay.
CHECK YOURSELF
If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-10
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Consumer surplus is the difference between a buyer's willingness to pay and the price actually paid. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Demand can be interpreted as buyers' marginal willingness to pay. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a buyer's willingness to pay and the market price actually paid.
Individual consumer surplus equals willingness to pay minus price.
On a graph, consumer surplus is the area below demand and above the market price up to the quantity traded.
A buyer whose willingness to pay is below price does not purchase and earns no consumer surplus.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume every trade creates surplus. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING CONSUMER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.

At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The demand intercept of $30 represents the highest willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is the triangle above price and below demand: 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is the rectangle below market price not consumer surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-11
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the seller's willingness to accept. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a seller's willingness to accept or marginal cost and the price received.
Individual producer surplus equals price received minus willingness to accept.
On a graph, producer surplus is the area above supply and below the market price up to the quantity traded.
A seller whose cost exceeds the market price does not make that trade.
WATCH OUT
Producer surplus is the price received minus willingness to accept, summed over units sold. Do not confuse this per-unit price-cost gap with total revenue.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING PRODUCER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The supply intercept is $6, so producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is the full area above supply not producer surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-12
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. Each trade adds to total surplus when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's opportunity cost. Total surplus is maximized when every mutually beneficial trade occurs and no trade with a cost above its value is completed.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Add consumer surplus and producer surplus to obtain total surplus.
For each possible trade, compare the buyer's willingness to pay with the seller's opportunity cost.
A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.
On a graph, total surplus is the area between demand and supply up to the quantity traded.
WATCH OUT
Total surplus adds consumer and producer surplus. A payment between buyers and sellers changes its distribution; a trade whose cost exceeds buyer value reduces total surplus.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TOTAL SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
The graph's equilibrium is 8 units at $14. Consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64, and producer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32. Total surplus is therefore $64 + $32 = $96.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyer value is $17 and seller cost is $22. Efficient action?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Efficient Quantity & Allocation
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Efficient Quantity & Allocation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The efficient quantity includes every unit whose buyer value is at least as large as its opportunity cost. Efficiency pairs the highest-value buyers with the lowest-cost sellers and continues exchange while the next buyer's willingness to pay covers the next seller's cost. Producing beyond that point destroys surplus, while stopping before it leaves gains unrealized.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Order potential trades from the highest buyer value and the lowest seller cost.
Complete every trade for which willingness to pay is at least as large as opportunity cost.
Stop when the next seller's cost exceeds the next buyer's value.
An efficient allocation sends the good to the highest-value buyers and production to the lowest-cost sellers.
WATCH OUT
More output is not always more efficient. Stop when the next unit costs more to produce than its buyer is willing to pay.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING THE EFFICIENT QUANTITY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 18 at quantity 0 and reaches price 2 at quantity 16. Upward-sloping S starts at price 2 and reaches price 18 at quantity 16. They intersect at E, quantity 8 and price 10, with dashed guides to the axes. Demand lies above supply to the left of E and below supply to its right.

Demand and supply intersect at 8 units and $10. At that quantity, the marginal buyer's value equals the marginal seller's cost. Units below 8 create positive gains from trade; units above 8 cost more than buyers value them. The efficient allocation therefore produces 8 units.
CHECK YOURSELF

Five buyers value one pass each at $27, $23, $18, $13, and $8. Five sellers have costs of $4, $10, $15, $21, and $25. How many trades create nonnegative gains, and why should the next trade not occur?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price or policy change can transfer surplus between buyers and sellers and can destroy surplus by preventing mutually beneficial trades. A transfer changes who receives existing gains without changing their total. Deadweight loss is different: it represents gains from exchange that disappear because quantity moves away from the efficient level.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Establish the initial consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus before the change.
Recalculate those areas after the price change or policy intervention.
Separate transfers between buyers and sellers from surplus that disappears entirely.
Deadweight loss represents mutually beneficial trades prevented by the change.
WATCH OUT
A demand curve and price are enough to calculate consumer surplus. A change in consumer surplus alone does not establish the change in producer surplus, total surplus, or deadweight loss.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING A CHANGE IN CONSUMER SURPLUS

Demand slopes from price 20 at zero quantity to zero at 20. At price 12 quantity is 8 and the consumer-surplus triangle is 32. At price 8 quantity is 12 and the larger consumer-surplus triangle is 72. Distinct hatching marks these overlapping areas. No supply curve, producer surplus or deadweight loss is claimed.

At price P1 = $12, quantity is 8 and consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($20 - $12) = $32. At P2 = $8, quantity rises to 12 and consumer surplus becomes 1/2 x 12 x ($20 - $8) = $72. The price decrease raises consumer surplus by $40. These demand-side areas do not identify a transfer or deadweight loss without supply-side information.
CHECK YOURSELF
Consumer surplus rises from $32 to $72 after a price decrease. What is the gain, and can this information alone establish the change in total surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-15
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Efficiency concerns the size of total surplus, while equity concerns how benefits and costs are distributed. The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use total surplus to evaluate efficiency and distributional evidence to evaluate equity.
Recognize that the allocation with the largest total surplus need not be the most equal.
Remember that measured willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay.
A policy judgment requires an explicit value choice when efficiency and equity point in different directions.
WATCH OUT
Efficiency compares total gains; equity evaluates their distribution. Greater total surplus does not by itself establish that a policy is fair.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING EFFICIENCY AND EQUITY

Policy A creates $500 of total surplus divided evenly between buyers and sellers. Policy B creates $520 of total surplus but gives $500 to sellers and $20 to buyers. Policy B is more efficient because total surplus is larger, but whether its distribution is more equitable is a separate normative judgment.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says efficiency requires equal gains. Correction?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
WATCH OUT

When the world price exceeds the domestic no-trade equilibrium price, domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. The difference is exports, not imports. Do not infer tariff revenue or deadweight loss from this free-trade example.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING EXPORTS

Horizontal axis: quantity of avocados in thousands; vertical axis: price of avocados in dollars. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up. They intersect at A, quantity 175 thousand and price 7. A horizontal world-price line marked Pw = $10 meets demand at 100 thousand and supply at 250 thousand. Dashed vertical guides show those quantities.

Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using the avocado export-market graph, what are domestic production, domestic consumption, and exports at Pw=$10?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-17
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

International trade changes consumer and producer surplus and creates net gains when the world price differs from the no-trade equilibrium price. The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.
Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume trade has only winners or only losers. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers. The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TRACING TRADE WINNERS AND LOSERS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Demand D falls from price 80 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 80. Supply S rises from price 20 and crosses D at quantity 30 and price 50. The horizontal world-price line Pw at price 30 meets S at quantity 10 and D at quantity 50; dashed vertical guides mark both quantities.

At the $30 world price, domestic producers supply 10 units and domestic consumers demand 50, so imports equal 40. Relative to the $50 no-trade equilibrium, the two gain-from-trade triangles each have base 20 and height 20. Their combined area is $200 + $200 = $400.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why do consumers gain when a lower world price opens an import market?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-18
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Economic cost includes both explicit payments and the implicit opportunity costs of owner-supplied resources. Explicit costs require cash payments to outside suppliers, while implicit costs measure the value of income or returns forgone by using the owner's time, money, or property in the business. Economic decisions count both because every resource has a next-best use.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Classify cash payments to outside suppliers as explicit costs.
Identify the income or return sacrificed on owner-supplied time, money, or property as an implicit cost.
Economic cost includes both explicit and implicit opportunity costs.
Do not treat an owner-supplied resource as free merely because no check is written.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to count only recorded expense. Economic cost equals explicit cost plus all implicit opportunity costs: $70,000 + $40,000 + $5,000.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COUNTING OPPORTUNITY COSTS

A business pays $70,000 in wages and rent. The owner also gives up a $40,000 salary and $5,000 of interest that invested capital could have earned elsewhere. Explicit cost is $70,000; implicit cost is $45,000; economic cost is $70,000 + $45,000 = $115,000.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which cost belongs in economic cost but not recorded accounting cost?
READY?

transcript.text: Accounting, Economic & Normal Profit
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-19
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate and interpret accounting profit, economic profit, implicit costs, and normal profit.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs from revenue, while economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs. Normal profit is the return required to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use, so it is included among implicit costs. Zero economic profit therefore means the firm covers every explicit and implicit cost, not that the owner receives nothing.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Start with total revenue and identify both explicit and implicit costs.
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs only; economic profit subtracts both kinds of cost.
Normal profit is the owner's opportunity cost and is included among implicit costs.
Zero economic profit can coexist with positive accounting profit.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat zero economic profit as failure. Zero economic profit includes normal compensation for owner resources. The $85,000 accounting profit exactly covers the $85,000 of implicit opportunity costs.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ACCOUNTING VERSUS ECONOMIC PROFIT

A firm earns $200,000 of revenue and pays $115,000 of explicit costs, so accounting profit is $85,000. If the owner's forgone salary, interest, and rent also total $85,000, economic profit is $85,000 - $85,000 = $0. The firm still earns normal profit because its resources receive their opportunity-cost return.
CHECK YOURSELF
A firm earns zero economic profit. What has it covered?

transcript.text: Short-Run Production & Diminishing Marginal Product
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-20
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Production & Diminishing Marginal Product.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In the short run, at least one input is fixed. Marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of a variable input. With fixed equipment, additional workers may eventually add less output than earlier workers. Diminishing marginal product means the addition falls; total product can still rise.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the fixed input and the variable input.
Marginal product is the change in total product from one more worker.
Diminishing marginal product begins when successive output additions fall.
Negative marginal product means another worker actually reduces total output.
WATCH OUT
Do not wait for marginal product to become negative. It is diminishing as soon as the next worker adds less output than the previous worker.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DIMINISHING MARGINAL PRODUCT

Total product rises from 34 units with three workers to 46 with four, so the fourth worker's marginal product is 12. The fifth worker raises output from 46 to 56, giving marginal product of 10. Output still increases, but the smaller addition shows diminishing marginal product.
CHECK YOURSELF
A sixth worker raises output from 56 to 64. Calculate that worker's marginal product. Is marginal product diminishing, and is total product still rising?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Cost Components & Cost Schedules
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-21
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Complete short-run cost schedules using total and average cost identities
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In the short run, total fixed cost (TFC) does not change with output, while total variable cost (TVC) rises or falls as production changes. Total cost combines both components: TC = TFC + TVC. For positive output Q, divide each total by Q: AFC = TFC / Q, AVC = TVC / Q, and ATC = TC / Q = AFC + AVC. At zero output, TVC is normally zero, TC equals TFC, and average costs are undefined because division by zero is impossible. On a total-cost graph, the vertical distance between TC and TVC equals TFC at every quantity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A cost-schedule row is missing TFC, TVC, or TC.
A fixed payment remains even when current output is zero.
A cost changes when labor, materials, or production changes.
The vertical gap between TC and TVC is compared across quantities.
Total costs must be converted to per-unit AFC, AVC, or ATC.
WATCH OUT

Do not subtract or multiply fixed and variable cost when finding total cost: add them. Also distinguish total fixed cost from average fixed cost. TFC stays constant as output changes, but AFC = TFC / Q falls as the same fixed amount is spread across more units. Average costs are not defined at Q = 0.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BUILDING A COST SCHEDULE

At Q = 120, TC is $1,200 and TVC is $800. TFC is the difference: $400. Divide each total by output to obtain AFC = $3.33, AVC = $6.67, and ATC = $10.00, rounded to cents. The completed row satisfies TC = TFC + TVC and ATC = AFC + AVC.
CHECK YOURSELF
At Q = 10, a schedule shows TFC = $90 and TC = $250. What are TVC, AFC, AVC, and ATC, and how can you verify that AFC + AVC = ATC?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.
Use per-unit measures only when output is positive.
WATCH OUT
Average costs are per unit; total costs are not. Subtract AVC from ATC to find AFC, then multiply AFC by positive output to recover total fixed cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING AVERAGE-COST CURVES

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: costs in dollars. Curves are labeled MC, AC and AVC. MC first dips slightly and then rises. It crosses AVC at its minimum, quantity 200 and cost 10. At quantity 400, MC crosses AC at its minimum of 20, while AVC is 12. Dashed guides mark the quantities and costs. AC remains above AVC.

At 400 units, the graph shows average cost of $20 and average variable cost of $12. Because AC = AVC + AFC, average fixed cost is $20 - $12 = $8 per unit. The gap between AC and AVC is therefore the firm's average fixed cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
At Q = 30, AVC is $14 and ATC is $24. Calculate AFC and total fixed cost. Verify your answer by multiplying the per-unit gap by output.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-23
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output. If labor is the only variable input and its wage is fixed, divide the added worker's wage by that worker's marginal product. Lower marginal product then means higher cost per extra unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for the change in total cost caused by producing one additional unit.
Compute marginal cost as the change in total cost divided by the change in output.
A fixed-cost change does not change marginal cost, but a variable-input cost change usually does.
When marginal product falls, marginal cost tends to rise if the input price is unchanged.
WATCH OUT
Hold the wage and other input conditions fixed when linking marginal product to marginal cost. A fixed-cost change alone does not change the cost of an extra unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: LINKING MARGINAL PRODUCT AND COST

Income Inequality & the Lorenz Curve
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-59
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret Lorenz curves, Gini coefficients, and redistribution tradeoffs.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income received by cumulative shares of the population, ordered from lowest to highest income. The 45-degree line represents complete equality. A curve farther below that line indicates greater inequality, not necessarily lower average income.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Read a point as a cumulative population share paired with a cumulative income share.
A Lorenz curve moving toward the equality line indicates less inequality.
The Gini coefficient summarizes the gap from equality: 0 is equality; values nearer 1 indicate more inequality.
Poverty thresholds and redistribution policies address related but distinct questions from inequality measurement.
WATCH OUT
Do not use a Lorenz curve to infer a country's income level. Two countries can have the same distribution shape and very different average incomes.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING A LORENZ CURVE

Horizontal axis: cumulative percentage of households; vertical axis: cumulative percentage of income. A dashed line of equality connects (0, 0) and (100, 100). Before Transfers, the Lorenz curve passes through (20, 5), (40, 15), (60, 30), (80, 55), and (100, 100). After Transfers, it passes through (20, 10), (40, 22), (60, 40), (80, 65), and (100, 100), closer to equality. Guides emphasize the bottom 40 percent shares of 15 and 22 percent. Printed Gini values are 0.380 before transfers and 0.252 after transfers.

Before transfers, the bottom 40 percent receives 15 percent of income. After transfers, its share rises to 22 percent and the Lorenz curve moves closer to equality. The displayed Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252. These changes indicate less relative inequality, but do not show whether total or average income rose.

transcript.text: Adverse Selection
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-60
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify hidden-information problems that arise before an agreement or transaction.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Adverse selection arises when one side has private information about characteristics or risk before an agreement. Because prices or terms cannot fully reflect each type, higher-risk or higher-cost participants may be more likely to enter, changing the market pool.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for hidden characteristics or risk known by one party before agreement.
The informed and uninformed sides value the transaction differently because information is unequal.
When one price covers many types, high-risk or high-cost types may participate disproportionately.
The pool can worsen, raising prices, reducing coverage, or eliminating beneficial trade.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse adverse selection with moral hazard. Adverse selection is hidden information before agreement; moral hazard is hidden action or changed behavior after protection.
WORKED EXAMPLE: AN INSURANCE RISK POOL
DIAGNOSE
hidden characteristics
before agreement
private risk
selection into the pool
market response

An insurer cannot perfectly observe applicants' health risk before enrollment, so it charges one premium based on average expected cost. Risk type already exists before coverage. Higher-risk applicants find the policy more attractive and enroll at a higher rate. The insured pool's expected cost rises, so the insurer may raise premiums or reduce coverage. Those responses can drive more low-risk buyers away, worsening selection.
CHECK YOURSELF
An applicant conceals a chronic condition before enrolling. Does the information problem occur before or after agreement?

transcript.text: Moral Hazard
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-61
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify how protection or a contract can change behavior after an agreement.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Moral hazard occurs when protection from some consequences changes a person's actions after an agreement, while those actions are difficult for the other party to observe or control. The protection changes incentives rather than merely revealing a preexisting type.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Coverage, a guarantee, or another agreement is already in place.
Behavior changes afterward because the person bears less of the consequence.
The relevant action or precaution is imperfectly observed or controlled.
Insurance, lending, employment, and guarantees can create this incentive.
WATCH OUT
Moral hazard is not simply bad behavior. Protection must change incentives after agreement. Hidden characteristics that exist before agreement instead point to adverse selection.
WORKED EXAMPLE: PRECAUTION AFTER COVERAGE
DIAGNOSE
after agreement
hidden action
protection
reduced precaution
changed incentives

A driver obtains collision insurance with a very low deductible. Coverage comes first. Because the insurer now pays most damage costs, the driver bears less of the financial consequence and becomes less careful about where the car is parked. That reduced incentive for precaution can raise expected losses. The mechanism is moral hazard because behavior changes after protection, not because the driver's type was hidden beforehand.
CHECK YOURSELF
After receiving a loan guarantee, a borrower chooses a riskier project. Does that change illustrate moral hazard?
